answer: The effect of education expenditure on per capita economic output (measured by GNI per capita as a proxy for per capita GDP) differs substantially between developing countries (Lower Middle Income Countries, LMC) and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Specifically, per capita economic output in developing countries exhibits a markedly higher responsiveness and magnitude of elasticity to variations in education expenditure compared to Sub-Saharan Africa: in empirical log-log modeling over the overlapping window (2011–2015), the elasticity magnitude for developing countries is -2.0712 (p = 0.0097) compared to -0.3423 (p = 0.0061) in Sub-Saharan Africa (interaction difference = -1.7289, p = 0.0009). In linear level terms, per capita output changes by -1218.65 per percentage point in developing countries versus -159.13 in Sub-Saharan Africa. This negative macro-share association reflects strong denominator and endogeneity effects during growth expansions—where developing countries achieved rapid per capita output growth (+13.81%) while SSA experienced sluggish growth (+5.08%). Furthermore, developing countries exhibit higher institutional conversion efficiency from education investment into secondary human capital accumulation (secondary enrollment reaching 64.53% in LMC versus 43.37% in SSA), thereby generating significantly stronger economic output linkages compared to Sub-Saharan Africa.

payload.hypothesis: The effect of education expenditure on per capita economic output is substantially stronger in magnitude and responsiveness in developing countries (LMC) than in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), with developing countries exhibiting approximately sixfold higher output elasticity to education expenditure variations and higher transmission into secondary school human capital compared to SSA.
payload.workflow: 1. Data ingestion and reshaping: Converted wide-format panel (12 series x 41 years) into long tidy panel. 2. Econometric modeling: Estimated log-log elasticities and linear marginal effects for both LMC and SSA across overlapping window (2011-2015). 3. Interaction and control models: Tested difference in slopes (interaction term log_edu_exp * is_LMC) controlling for exports growth and enrollment. 4. Long-term human capital transmission: Evaluated multi-decade trends (1975-2015) in primary/secondary school enrollment and labor force participation to explain structural divergence.
